title: Pair With Target Sum
statement:
A shop keeps a list of item prices. A customer wants exactly **two different items** whose prices add up to a given budget.

Find the pair that is *completed earliest*: among all valid pairs `(i, j)` with `i < j`, choose the one with the smallest `j`, and for that `j` the smallest `i`. Print the 1-based positions `i j`, or `-1` if no pair exists.
inputFormat: Line 1: `n t` (item count and budget). Line 2: `n` integers, the prices.
constraints: 2 ≤ n ≤ 100 000; prices and t fit in 32-bit signed integers.
hints: Checking every pair works but is too slow for large n.
While scanning left to right, what do you need to remember about the prices you have already seen?
A hash map from price to the first position it appeared turns the inner loop into one lookup.

title: Calm Stretch
statement:
A sensor reports one reading per minute. A stretch of consecutive minutes is **calm** if the highest and lowest readings in it differ by at most `k`.

Print the length of the longest calm stretch.
inputFormat: Line 1: `n k`. Line 2: `n` integers, the readings.
outputFormat: One integer: the longest calm stretch.
hints: Try a window that grows on the right and shrinks on the left.
To know the window's max and min quickly after the left side moves, what structure keeps them in order?
Two monotonic deques (one for the max, one for the min) give O(n) overall.

tests.explanation: Minutes 1-3 (4, 6, 5) differ by 2; no longer stretch qualifies.
A single reading is always calm.

title: Rotated Lookup
statement:
A sorted list of **distinct** integers was cut at some position and the two parts swapped, so it may look like `[40, 50, 10, 20, 30]`.

Given the rotated list and a value, print the 0-based position of the value, or `-1` if it is absent. Aim for logarithmic time.
hints: At any midpoint, at least one half of the range is still sorted.
Decide which half is sorted, then check whether the target can lie inside it.
Keep narrowing the range exactly like binary search.

title: Minimum Ship Capacity
statement:
Packages with given weights must be shipped **in the given order**. Each day the truck takes consecutive packages as long as their total weight fits its capacity. You have `d` days.

Print the smallest truck capacity that ships every package within `d` days.
inputFormat: Line 1: `n d`. Line 2: `n` positive integers, the weights.
hints: The capacity can never be below the heaviest package nor above the total weight.
If a capacity works, any larger one works too. What does that suggest?
Binary search the capacity; for each guess, greedily count the days needed.

tests.explanation: Capacity 9 gives days {4,2,3}, {7,1}, {5}; 8 would need four days.
One package per day, so the heaviest decides.

title: Balanced Brackets
statement:
A string is made only of the characters `(`, `)`, `[`, `]`, `{` and `}`. It is **balanced** when every opener is closed by the same kind of bracket in the correct order.

Print `YES` if the string is balanced, otherwise `NO`.
hints: The most recent unclosed opener must be closed first.
Which data structure gives you the most recent item?
Push openers; on a closer, the top of the stack must be its partner. Also check the stack is empty at the end.

title: Next Warmer Day
statement: For each day you are given the temperature. For every day, print how many days you must wait until a **strictly warmer** day arrives, or `0` if none ever does.
hints: For one day, scanning forward is O(n); doing it for all days is O(n²).
Keep days whose answer is still unknown in a stack.
When a warmer temperature arrives, pop every colder day and record the distance.

tests.explanation: Day 1 waits 3 days for 40; day 4 never sees warmer.

title: Merge Meeting Slots
statement:
A room booking system stores slots as `[start, end)` pairs. Slots that overlap **or touch** (one ends exactly when the next starts) should be shown as a single block.

Print the number of blocks, then each block as `start end`, ordered by start.
outputFormat: First line: the number of blocks. Then one line per block.
hints: Order matters: sort first.
After sorting by start, compare each slot only with the last merged block.
If it starts at or before the block's end, extend the block; otherwise start a new one.

tests.explanation: [1,3] and [2,6] merge to [1,6]; [6,7] touches it, giving [1,7]; [8,10] stays apart.

title: Subarrays With Sum
statement: Count the contiguous, non-empty subarrays whose elements add up to exactly `k`. Numbers may be negative, so a sliding window will not work.
hints: Let P[i] be the sum of the first i numbers. A subarray (i, j] has sum P[j] - P[i].
For each j you need how many earlier prefixes equal P[j] - k.
Store prefix-sum counts in a hash map as you scan.

tests.explanation: The subarrays at positions 1-2, 2-3, 3-4 and 4-5 each sum to 3.

title: Fewest Coins
statement: You have unlimited coins of several denominations. Print the **fewest coins** that add up to exactly `t`, or `-1` if it is impossible. A total of 0 needs 0 coins.
inputFormat: Line 1: `n t`. Line 2: `n` distinct coin values.
hints: Greedy (always the biggest coin) can fail. Think about smaller totals.
Let best[v] be the fewest coins for total v.
best[v] = 1 + min(best[v - c]) over coins c ≤ v.

tests.explanation: Odd totals cannot be formed from even coins.

title: Staircase Ways
statement: A staircase has `n` steps. You may climb 1, 2 or 3 steps at a time. Print the number of distinct ways to reach the top, modulo 1 000 000 007.
hints: The last move was 1, 2 or 3 steps.
ways[i] = ways[i-1] + ways[i-2] + ways[i-3].
Remember to take the modulo at every addition.

title: Longest Common Run
statement: Two strings are given. Print the length of the longest sequence of characters that appears in **both**, in the same order (characters need not be adjacent).
hints: Compare prefixes: what happens when the last characters match?
dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 if they match, else max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]).
You only need the previous row to compute the next.

title: Island Counter
statement: A map is a grid of `#` (land) and `.` (water). Land cells touching horizontally or vertically belong to the same island. Print the number of islands.
inputFormat: Line 1: `h w`. Then `h` lines of `w` characters.
hints: When you find land, everything connected to it is one island.
Walk the island with DFS or BFS and mark its cells as visited.
Count how many times you start a new walk.

tests.explanation: Two islands: the top-left group and the right-hand pair.

title: Shortest Maze Path
statement: A maze has open cells, walls `#`, a start `S` and an exit `E`. You move one step up, down, left or right through open cells. Print the minimum number of steps from `S` to `E`, or `-1`.
inputFormat: Line 1: `h w`. Then `h` lines of `w` characters.
constraints: 2 ≤ h, w ≤ 500; exactly one S and one E.
hints: All moves cost the same, so the first time you reach a cell is the shortest way.
Which traversal explores in order of distance?
Breadth-first search with a queue and a distance per cell.

tests.explanation: Go down twice, then right three times.
The wall column blocks every route.

title: Course Order
statement: A degree has `n` courses numbered 1..n and `m` rules `a b`, meaning course `a` must be taken before `b`. Print an order that respects every rule. If several orders work, print the one that is smallest when compared number by number. Print `IMPOSSIBLE` if the rules contain a cycle.
hints: A course with no unmet prerequisite can be taken now.
Track in-degrees; courses at 0 are ready.
Use a min-heap for the ready set so the smallest label is always chosen. If fewer than n courses get taken, there is a cycle.

tests.explanation: Each course needs the other first.

title: Cheapest Route
statement: A country has `n` cities and `m` two-way roads with positive tolls. Print the cheapest total toll from city 1 to city `n`, or `-1` if there is no route.
inputFormat: Line 1: `n m`. Then `m` lines `a b w`.
hints: Tolls are positive, so the cheapest known city can be finalised.
Use a priority queue keyed by distance (Dijkstra).
Skip a popped entry whose distance is already outdated.

title: Most Meetings
statement: One room, many requests `[start, end)`. Two meetings may share an endpoint (one ends when the next begins). Print the **largest number** of meetings that can be held without overlap.
hints: Which meeting should you choose first?
The one that ends earliest leaves the most room.
Sort by end time and take every meeting that starts at or after the last chosen end.

tests.explanation: Take [1,3) and [3,5), or [2,4) and [4,6): at most 2.

title: Fewest Hops
statement: You stand on the first of `n` stepping stones. Stone `i` lets you jump **up to** `a[i]` stones forward. Print the fewest jumps needed to reach the last stone, or `-1` if it cannot be reached.
hints: Think in layers: all stones reachable with 1 jump, then 2 jumps, and so on.
Track the farthest stone reachable from the current layer.
When you pass the end of the current layer, take one more jump.

tests.explanation: Jump to stone 2, then to the end: 2 hops.

title: Kth Largest
statement: Print the `k`-th largest value in a list of numbers (duplicates count separately: in `[5, 5, 3]` the 2nd largest is 5).
hints: Sorting works in O(n log n).
You only need to remember the k biggest values seen so far.
Keep a min-heap of size k; its top is the answer.

title: Anagram Groups
statement: Words are anagrams if they use exactly the same letters the same number of times. Print how many **groups of mutually anagram words** the list splits into.
inputFormat: Line 1: `n`. Line 2: `n` words separated by spaces.
hints: Two anagrams look identical once their letters are sorted.
Use the sorted letters (or letter counts) as a hash key.
The answer is the number of distinct keys.

tests.explanation: Two groups: {listen, silent, enlist} and {google, gogole}.

tests.input:
6
cbc ccbc cb acc b aabc

8
a cca c abbb ccca bb abac acc

6
b cc abcb accc ca a

title: Longest Unique Stretch
statement: Print the length of the longest substring in which **no character repeats**.
hints: Maintain a window with no repeats.
When a character repeats, move the left edge past its previous position.
Store the last index of each character.

tests.explanation: `abc` has length 3 and nothing longer is repeat-free.

title: Subset Target Count
statement: Count the subsets of a list (chosen by position, so equal values in different places count separately; the empty subset counts) whose sum equals `t`.
hints: For each element you choose: take it or leave it.
Recurse on the rest with the remaining target.
At the end of the list, a match is exactly when the remaining target is 0.

title: Trapped Rainwater
statement: Bars of width 1 and given heights stand side by side. After rain, water collects between them. Print the total units of trapped water.
hints: Water above a bar is limited by the lower of the tallest bar on its left and on its right.
Precomputing both maxima works in O(n) extra space.
Two pointers moving inward let you do it in O(1) space: always advance the side with the smaller wall.

tests.explanation: Positions 2, 3 and 4 hold 3, 1 and 3 units of water: 7 in total.

title: Edit Distance
statement: Turn string `a` into string `b` using the fewest operations, where one operation inserts, deletes or replaces a single character. Print that minimum.
hints: Look at the last character of each string.
If equal, no cost; otherwise consider insert, delete and replace.
dp[i][j] = 1 + min of the three neighbours; one row is enough.

tests.explanation: Replace k, replace e, insert g: 3.

title: Friend Circles
statement: `n` people start with no friends. Then `m` friendships `a b` are announced; friendship is transitive for the purposes of a **circle** (a group connected through any chain of friends). Print the number of circles after all announcements.
hints: Every merge of two different circles reduces the count by one.
How can you quickly tell whether two people are already in the same circle?
Disjoint-set union with path compression.

title: Largest Skyline Rectangle
statement: A skyline is a row of adjacent bars of width 1. Find the area of the largest axis-aligned rectangle that fits entirely inside the skyline.
inputFormat: Line 1: `n`. Line 2: `n` non-negative integers, the bar heights.
hints: For each bar, how far can a rectangle of exactly its height extend left and right?
The extension stops at the nearest shorter bar on each side.
A monotonic stack finds both boundaries in one pass.

tests.explanation: Bars of height 5 and 6 form a 5×2 = 10 rectangle.

title: Even or Odd
statement: Read an integer and print `EVEN` if it is divisible by 2, otherwise `ODD`.
hints: What is the remainder when you divide by 2?
Be careful with negative numbers: -3 is odd.

title: Leap Year Check
statement: A year is a leap year if it is divisible by 4, except century years, which must be divisible by 400. Print `YES` or `NO`.
hints: Apply the three rules in order.
1900 is not a leap year but 2000 is.

tests.explanation: Divisible by 4 and not a century year.
A century year not divisible by 400.

title: Count Digits
statement: Print how many digits the non-negative integer `n` has (0 has one digit).
hints: Repeatedly divide by 10.
Treat 0 as a special case.

title: Sum of Digits
statement: Print the sum of the decimal digits of `n`.
hints: `n % 10` is the last digit.
Drop it with integer division by 10.

title: Reverse a Number
statement: Print the number formed by reversing the digits of non-negative `n` (drop leading zeros of the result).
hints: Build the result digit by digit: `rev = rev * 10 + last`.

title: Palindrome Number
statement: Print `YES` if the non-negative integer reads the same forwards and backwards, otherwise `NO`.
hints: Compare the number with its reversal.

title: Factorial
hints: Multiply 1..n, taking the modulo after each step.

title: Nth Fibonacci Number
statement: With F(0)=0, F(1)=1 and F(n)=F(n-1)+F(n-2), print F(n) modulo 1 000 000 007.
hints: Keep only the last two values.
Take the modulo at each addition.

title: GCD of Two Numbers
statement: Print the greatest common divisor of two positive integers.
hints: Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b).

tests.explanation: The largest number dividing both is 6.

title: LCM of Two Numbers
statement: Print the least common multiple of two positive integers.
hints: lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) × b.

tests.explanation: 12 is the smallest number both divide.

title: Prime Number Check
statement: Print `YES` if `n` is prime, otherwise `NO`.
hints: Only test divisors up to √n.
1 is not prime.

title: Count Primes Up To N
statement: Print how many prime numbers are ≤ `n`.
hints: Testing each number separately is slow.
The Sieve of Eratosthenes crosses out multiples of each prime.

tests.explanation: There are no primes up to 1.

title: Perfect Number Check
statement: A number is **perfect** if it equals the sum of its proper divisors (excluding itself). Print `YES` or `NO`.
hints: Add the divisors from 1 to n/2, or pair them up to √n.

tests.explanation: The proper divisors add up to 16.

title: Decimal to Binary
statement: Print the binary representation of the non-negative integer `n` without leading zeros (print `0` for 0).
hints: Repeatedly divide by 2 and collect remainders (in reverse).

title: Power of Two Check
statement: Print `YES` if `n` is a power of two (1, 2, 4, 8, ...), otherwise `NO`.
hints: A power of two has exactly one bit set.
`n & (n - 1)` clears the lowest set bit.

title: Sum of Array Elements
statement: Print the sum of all numbers in the array.
hints: Keep a running total.

title: Second Largest Element
statement: Print the second largest **distinct** value, or `-1` if there is none.
hints: Track the largest and second largest in one pass.
Equal values do not count twice.

tests.explanation: Distinct values are 2, 4, 7, 9; the second largest is 7.

title: Count Even and Odd Numbers
statement: Print the number of even values and the number of odd values, separated by a space.
hints: Check each value's remainder mod 2 (negative numbers too).

title: Reverse an Array
statement: Print the array in reverse order, separated by spaces.
hints: Swap from both ends moving inward.

title: Check if an Array Is Sorted
statement: Print `YES` if the array is in non-decreasing order, otherwise `NO`.
hints: Compare each element with the next.

title: Count Vowels
statement: Print how many vowels (`a e i o u`, case-insensitive) the text contains.
hints: Normalise to lower case, then count.

title: Palindrome String Check
statement: Print `YES` if the string (letters only, lower case) reads the same both ways, otherwise `NO`.
hints: Compare characters from both ends moving inward.

title: Count Words in a Sentence
statement: Words are separated by one or more spaces. Print how many words the line contains.
hints: Split on whitespace and count the non-empty parts.

tests.explanation: Four words; extra spaces do not count.

tests.input: www www www ww www www
ww  ww  ww  w  ww  ww
ww   www   w   www   ww   w

title: Toggle Case
statement: Swap the case of every letter (upper to lower and lower to upper); other characters stay the same.
hints: Use the language's case helpers or add/subtract 32 on ASCII letters.

tests.explanation: Letters flip, the rest is unchanged.

title: Sum of First N Numbers
statement: Print 1 + 2 + ... + n. Practise writing it recursively: sum(n) = n + sum(n - 1).
hints: Base case: sum(0) = 0.
A closed formula also exists: n(n+1)/2.

title: Largest of Three
statement: Print the largest of three integers.
hints: Compare in pairs.

title: Trailing Zeroes of a Factorial
statement: Print how many zeroes `n!` ends with.
hints: A zero comes from a factor 10 = 2 × 5.
There are always more 2s than 5s, so count the 5s: n/5 + n/25 + ...

title: Armstrong Number
statement: A number is an **Armstrong number** if it equals the sum of its digits each raised to the power of the number of digits (153 = 1³ + 5³ + 3³). Print `YES` or `NO`.
hints: Count the digits first.
